full_judgment:
c.	Accused Noor Alam was apprehended by police on 31-8-1999. He on 1-9-1999 made confessional statement under sections 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (shortly The Code) before Md Sabir Ahmed, Magistrate, First Class, Khulna (PW 35) confessing his guilt and implicated himself, condemned prisoners, convict-appellants and others in commission of crime. Accused Noor Alam, thereafter, had chosen to be an approver and stood in witness box as PW 6. He generated detailed disclosure of offence committed by condemned prisoners and convict-appellants and accredited parts performed by condemned prisoners and convict-appellants in murdering Fatik and in removing the evidence of crime. 

 8. Central evidence connecting condemned prisoners and convict-appellants in the commission of crime consisted of testimonies of Informant PW 1 Md Ahasanul Kabir who gave prosecution version and proved First Information Report, PW 3 Md Zalal Uddin, Assistant Engineer, T &T Division, Khulna who was in-charge of Divisional Engineer in the month of December, 1999 who proved that telephone number being 723777 of Khodeja Begum was changed and a new number being 732377 had been installed on acceptance of fees of change, PW 4 Sk Modasser Hossain, a seizure list witness to seizure of petition filed in respect of change of telephone number, PW 5 Md Kamrul Islam son-in-law of PW 36 Hashem Ali Molla who testified that his father-in-Iaw (PW 36) laid bare that Fatik went out of the house with Abdus Sabur and on the eve of departure Abdus Sabur supplied telephone No. 723777 with him, PW 6 Nur Alam, bodyguard of Ershad Ali Sikder who gave a vivid account of occurrence leading to murder of Fatik and also disappearance of his body, PW 7 Mollah Zafar Ali, Office Assistant of Khulna Divisional Telephone Office who was a witness to petition filed for changing the telephone number of Khodeja Begum, wife of Ershad Ali Sikder, PW 24 Dr Sayed Mahabub Hafiz, Assistant Professor, Forensic Medicine, Khulna Medical College Hospital who examined eighty-seven (87) pieces of bones and recorded opinion that out of twenty-six (26) bones there was one human bone, PW 35 Md Sabir Ahmed, Metropolitan Magistrate, First Class, Khulna who recorded judicial confessional statement of Noor Alam (approver PW 6), PW 36 Md Hashem Ali Molla, father of Fatik who in his evidence disclosed the facts of two telephone calls and departure of Fatik with Abdus Sabur and, also, demand of Taka 5,00,000 and PW 37 Satara Begum, mother of Fatik, who, also, testified the fact of two telephone calls and departure of her son Fatik with Abdus Sabur and, also, demand of Taka 10,00.000 from them on condition of recovery of her son Fatik. 

 I .On the strength of section 133 read with section 114(b) of The Evidence Act the testimony of PW 6 Noor Alam could be relied upon to be trustworthy and there could not be any legal bar in coming to a decision on the basis of testimony of PW 6. 

 In counting reasons learned Trial Judge meditated sections 133 and 114(b) of The Evidence Act and took into stock legal implication of two sections of The Evidence Act. 

 III.Prosecution stood proved by the following evidences and circumstances: 

 a. 	In ascertainment of presence of victim Fatik in the house telephone call by Abdus Sabur between 10-00 AM-10-30 AM which had been proved by evidence of PW 36 and PW 37. 

 b.	Calling of victim Fatik by Khodeja Begum through telephone at about 11-00 AM which had been established by evidence of PW 6 and stood corroborated and supported by evidence of PW 36 and PW 37. 

 d.	Arrival of Fatik in the house of Khodeja Begum at about 12-00 noon which was proved by evidence of PW 36. 

 10. Sustainability of conviction and sentence has been assailed pressing into service the contention from side of condemned prisoners and convict-appellant Idris Jamai that conviction and sentence had been based on confessional statement of approver PW 6 and his testimony in Court as PW 6 and the said testimony had not been corroborated by any other testimonies and, also, by other circumstantial evidences and conviction and sentence based upon uncorroborated testimony of approver PW 6 is neither safe nor proper and conviction and sentence cannot be sustained at all. 

 12. Repelling the contentions advanced, it is contended from side of State that testimony of approver PW 6 stood sufficiently corroborated by testimonies of PWs. 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 36 and 37 and change of telephone of Khodeja Begum on 13-4-1998 is sufficient evidence connecting condemned prisoners and accused-appellants in' crime and no material discrepancies is manifested in testimonies of PW 36 and PW 37 and discrepancies in respect of demand of Taka 5,00,000 or Taka 10,00,000, Taka 5,00,000 by PW 36 and Taka 10,00,000 by PW 37, cannot at all strike at the root of prosecution case and convict-appellant Abdus Sabur had been sufficiently identified and marked as the person who took victim Fatik outside the house. 

 1.	Whether awarding of conviction and sentence upon condemned prisoners and convict-appellants can be sustained on evidences, materials on record and in safe dispensation of criminal justice. 

 14. The answer to the questions posed definitely will be inevitably founded upon intensive appraisal of our legal survey of law on the subject and evidence of PW 6 and other evidences and confessional statement of PW 6 and fact and circumstances of case. 

 18. Section 201 of the Penal Code relates to disappearance of evidence of commission of offence and includes also giving of false information with intention of screening an offender. The underlying object of section 201 is two-fold: " 

 (i) 	to punish person causing disappearance of evidence of an offence committed with intention of screening offender from punishment and 

 2.	  Evidence of PW 35 Metropolitan Magistrate, First Class, Khulna who recorded Judicial confessional statement of No or Alam PW 6. 

 3.	Evidence of approver PW 6 Noor Alam. 

 4.	Evidence of PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 24, 36 and 37. 

 5.	Judicial confessional statement of PW 6 and evidence of PW 35. 

 20. Confession is nothing but admission of guilt by accused. Confession of an accused is not an evidence as defined in section 3 of The Evidence Act. Under section 30 confession of a co-accused can be taken into consideration but cannot be treated as a substantive evidence and can be pressed into service in support of other evidences. PW 6 made confession rendering a disclosure of place, time, manner of crime and, also, brought about vivid disclosure 'of the specific parts played by condemned prisoners and convict-appellants. 

 24. Illustration (b) to section 114 of The Evidence Act runs thus: 

 "114. (a) 	.............. 

 25. Taylor; in his Treatise on the Law of Evidence-(1931), Vol 1 paragraph 967 observed: 

 "Accomplices who are usually interested, and always infamous witnesses, and whose testimony is admitted from necessity, it being often impossible, without having recourse to such evidence, to bring the principal offenders to justice." 

 26. The combined effect of section 133 and section 114, illustration (b) of The Evidence Act is that an accomplice is competent to give evidence but it would be unsafe to convict the accused upon his testimony alone. Though conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal, yet Courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence of such a witness without corroboration in material particulars. 

 There is no doubt that the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice is admissible in law (R v James Atwood) (1787) 1 Leach 464=168 ER 334). But it has been long a rule of practice at common law for the Judge to warn the jury of the danger of convicting a prisoner on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice, and in the discretion of the Judge, to advise them not to convict upon such evidence, but the Judge should point out to the jury that it is within their legal province to convict upon such unconfirmed evidence (R v Stubbs: 1885 Dears CC 555 Meunier, 1n Re(1894 2 QB 415). 

 28. In Bhuboni Sahu vs R. AIR 1949 PC 257 = 50 CrilJ 872 Privy Council after noticing section 133 and illustration (b) to section 114 of The Evidence Act observed: 

 whilst it is not illegal to act on the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice, it is a rule of prudence so universally followed as to amount almost to a rule of law that it is unsafe to act on the evidence of an accomplice unless it is corroborated in material respects so as to implicate the accused; and further that the evidence of one accomplice cannot be used to corroborate the evidence of another accomplice. The rule of prudence was based on the interpretation of the phrase 'corroborated in material particulars' in illustration (b). Delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee, Sir John Beaumont observed that the danger of acting on accomplice evidence is not merely that the accomplice is on his own admission a man of bad character who took part in the offence and afterwards to save himself betrayed his former associates, and who has placed himself in a position in which he can hardly fail to have a strong bias in favour of the prosecution; the real danger is that he is telling a story which in its general outline is true, and it is easy for him to work into the story-matter which is untrue. He may implicate ten people in an offence and the story may be true in all its details as to eight of them but untrue as to the other two whose names may have been introduced because they are enemies of the approver. The only real safeguard therefore, against the risk of condemning the innocent with the guilty lies in insisting on independent evidence which in some measure implicates each accused. 

 29. For corroborative evidence Court must look at the broad spectrum of the approver's version and then find out whether there is other evidence to corroborate and lend assurance to that version. The nature and extent of such corroboration may depend upon the facts of different cases. Corroboration need not be in the form of ocular testimony of witnesses and may even be in the form of circumstantial evidence. It is to be borne in mind that the evidence of approver is held to be trustworthy, must be shown that the story given by approver so far as an accused is concerned, must implicate him in such a manner as to give rise to a conclusion of guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Insistence upon corroboration is based on the rule of caution and not merely a rule of law. 

 31. We shall now address ourselves to point how far the confessional statement and evidence of approver PW 6 stood corroborated by other evidences such as evidence of PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 36 and 37. 

 Version of approver PW 6 discloses that on 5-4-1998 he went to condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder's house. He went to bed at 9-00 AM -10-00 AM. He heard sound of beating. On the following day i.e. on 6-4-1998 at about 8-00 AM - 9-00 AM he woke up and found that Ershad Ali Sikder putting pistol to the head of Khodeja Begum ordered her to call victirn Fatik over telephone and from telephone No. 723777 Khodeja Begum made telephone call. Ershad Ali Sikder then from telephone No. 723777 called condemned prisoner Liaquat Lashkar and Jamai Farook. Ershad Ali Sikder asked Khodeja Begum to take victim Fatik upstairs at about 11-30 AM. Fatik reached the house. Khodeja Begum took him on the upstairs of the building. Ershad Ali Sikder pointed his pistol on .the chest of Fatik. Evidence of approver PW 6 further revealed that at about 7-00 PM-800 PM Fatik was carried down to ground floor of the building and he was taken to ice factory situated at ghat (Landing Space) No.5. Ershad Ali Sikder stood on the chest of Fatik and gave him kicks and broke his bones. Fatik died and dead body of Fatik was placed in a bag and along with two freezed cement bags dead body of Fatik was thrown into the river. 

 34. It is in the evidence of PW 3 Md Zalal Uddin that telephone No. 723777 stood in the name of Khodeja Begum who applied for change of telephone number and deposited Taka 5,000 for the purpose 'of transfer and a new telephone No. 732377 had been installed. In cross-examination he stated that the petition for transfer of the telephone had been submitted on 13-4-1998. PW 4 Sk Modasser Hossain, another Assistant Engineer in the Office of PW 3 gave evidence that CID police seized the application by which telephone No. 723777 had been changed and seizure list, was prepared and he is a witness to seizure PW 7 Mollah Zafar AIi, who is an Office Assistant, testified in his testimony that Khodeja Begum, wife of Ershad Ali Sikder, laid a petition for change of telephone number and that petition was seized by police. 

 35. From evidence of PW 3, Assistant Engineer of T &T, Khulna Division, PW 4, another Assistant Engineer, T&T, Khulna Division and PW 7, Office Assistant of Khulna Division, Telecom Office, Khulna, it came out that telephone No. 723777 was on receipt of Taka 5,000 changed and in place of that telephone, telephone being 732377 had been installed. 

 36. It came to light from the evidence of PW 6 Noor Alam that, Ershad Ali Sikder pointed a pistol to the head of his wife Khodeja Begum and ordered her to have a telephone call to Fatik and Khodeja Begum made it telephone call from. telephone No. 723777 and Fatik arrived at the house at about 11-00 AM or 11-30AM on 6-4-1998. 

 37. PW 36 Md Hashem Ali Mollah gave version that on 6-4-1998 his son Fatik came to his residence in Khulna from Dhaka at 8-30 AM and accused Abdus Sabur inquired of arrival of Fatik over telephone and, thereafter, victim Fatik talked to Abdus Sabur over telephone. Further version came out that after half an hour at about 11-00 AM another telephone call came and Fatik received the said telephone call and after about 10/15 minutes Abdus Sabur physically made his appearance in the house and Fatik and Abdus together went out of the house towards Khulna by a baby taxi. PW 36 in his evidence also, disclosed that Abdus Sabur supplied telephone No. 723777 and said that he would be available on the said telephone and after the disappearance of Fatik attempt was made to talk over the said telephone No. 723777 but no response came. This witness, stated that he became aware that the telephone was of Ershad Ali Sikder. 

 38. PW 37 Satara Begum, mother of victim Fatik, gave evidence in the similar language and terms which is that on 6-4-1998 her son Fatik arrived in Khulna from Dhaka in connection with before Eid-ul Azha. At about 10-30 AM a telephone call came and her husband (PW 36) handed over telephone to his son Fatik and Fatik talked to Abdus Sabur over telephone. After about half an hour another telephone call came and Fatik himself received the call. Abdus Sabur came to their house and her son Fatik and Abdus Sabur left the house towards Khulna. 

 39. PW. 5 Md Kamrul Islam in his evidence stated that on 7-4-1998 on being summoned he went to the house of his father-in-law (PW 36) and there he heard from both his father-in-law and mother-in-law that on 6-4-1998 Fatik came to Khulna house from Dhaka and with Abdus Sabur at about 11-30 AM went out of the house and Abdus Sabur before departure supplied telephone No. 723777. 

 40. Occurrence took place on 6-4-1998. First Information Report was lodged on 9-4-1998. Event of change of telephone took place on 13-4-1998 i.e. after a period of only four days of laying of First Information Report. Condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder anticipated and could foresee that in the event of supply of his telephone number 723777 by Abdus Sabur to father of Fatik Md Hashem Ali Mollah (PW 36) and the use of telephone by him and Khodeja Begum that telephone No. 723777 would be an incriminating evidence and circumstances against him and to wipe out that incriminating evidence and circumstances condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder promptly took efforts in the matter of changing of telephone No. 723777 and installed a new telephone No. 732377. Mens rea, thus, appeared to have very much worked in the mind of condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder. 

 41. Circumstantial evidence is not direct to the point in issue, but consists of evidence of various other facts which are so closely associated with the fact in issue that taken together, they form a chain of circumstances from which the existence of the principal fact can be legally inferred or presumed. For a crime to be proved, it is not necessary that the crime must be seen to have been committed and must, in all circumstances, be proved by direct ocular evidence by examining before the Court those persons who had seen its commission. The offence can be proved by circumstantial evidence also. The principal fact or "factum probandum" must be. proved indirectly by means of certain inferences drawn from "factum probandum, that is, the probative or evidentiary fact. 

 42. Confessional statement of approver PW 6 was proved by PW 35 Metropolitan Magistrate, First Class, Khulna. Evidence of approver PW 6 connecting condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder in commission of crime and evidences of PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 36 and 37 created such a chain in themselves which led to the conclusion that condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder is the perpetrator who caused death of Fatik and, thereafter, brought into existence the disappearance of evidence of offence. Common intention on the part of condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder could not be proved and substantiated and he cannot be liable to be convicted for offence of sections 302/34 of the Penal Code but the offence of sections 302/201 had been clearly proved and established. Prosecution, thus, could bring home offence of sections 302/201 of the Penal Code and not of section 34 of The Code to the door of condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder by evidence of approver PW 6 which lent support to other evidences stated above. 

 Except the testimony of approver PW 6 here were no evidence, whether ocular or circumstantial whatsoever, to connect condemned prisoners Liaquat Lashkar and Jamai Farooq and convict-appellant Idris Jamai. It is posited here that simply on the basis of a solitary testimony of approver PW 6, whose evidence can be viewed as an evidence of traitor, condemned prisoners Liaquat Lashkar and Jamai Farooq and convict-appellant Idris Jamai could not be and cannot be convicted for the charges mounted against them. Prosecution failed to bring home the offence of sections 302/201/34 of the Penal Code against condemned prisoners Liaquat Lashkar and Jamai Farooq and convict-appellant Idris Jamai and they are entitled to be favoured with a verdict of acquittal. Trial Judge was not at all justified in awarding conviction and sentence upon condemned prisoners Liaquat Lashkar and Jamai Farooq and convict-appellant Idris Jamai of the charges levelled against them. Contention pressed into service from the side of condemned prisoners Ershad Ali Sikder, Liaquat Lashkar and Jamai Farooq and convict-appellant ldris Jamai stands disposed of in the terms stated above. 

 It is in the evidence of Informant PW 1 that convict-appellant Abdus Sabur at about 11-30-12-00 AM took Md Jahangir Kabir alias Fatik to Khulna and Fatik remained untraced and subsequently on 7-4-1998 convict-appellant Abdus Sabur along with Shandha came to their house and gave inmates of the house consolation that Fatik would come back and nothing to be worried. It is, also, in his evidence that on 8-4-1998 at about 8-00 AM Abdus Sabur and Shandha again came to their house and disclosed that whereabouts of Fatik could be disclosed on payment of Taka 5,00,000. 

 45. PW 36 in his evidence stated that on 6-4-1998 his son Fatik came from Dhaka at about 8-30 to 9-00 AM A. telephone call came in their telephone No. 760934 and he received the telephone call and from the other side Abdus Sabur inquired of arrival of his son Fatik in his house and he called Fatik and Fatik and Abdus Sabur had telephonic conversation. Abdus Sabur, thereafter, himself approached in his house and his son Fatik and Abdus Sabur had conversation and they together by a baby-taxi proceeded towards Khulna. He made a query as to where they were going. Abdus Sabur supplied telephone No. 723777 and told him that they would be available over that telephone. It is, also, in his testimony that on the previous day of Eid-ul-Azha Abdus Sabur along with Sandha came to his house and demand Taka 5,00,000. 

 47. From clinching evidences of PW 1, PW 36 and PW 37 it demonstratively came out that Abdus Sabur had a telephone conversation with Fatik and following telephone talk Abdus Sabur came to the house of PW 36 and Abdus Sabur and Fatik had discussion and, thereafter, both of them came out of the house and proceeded towards Khulna by a babytaxi. It has been, also, clearly established by evidences that Abdus Sabur put forward a claim of Taka 5,00,000 as evidenced by PW 1 and PW 36 and condition was put forward that in the event of payment of that money Fatik would be recovered. Complicity of Abdus Sabur in the offence, thus. became crystallised. 

 48. Abdus Sabur though might not have been present at the time of commission of crime and at the scene of offence he took Fatik from his house to the house of Ershad Ali Sikder and Khodeja Begum. Fatik was killed in ice factory of Ershad Ali Sikder as emerged from the evidence of approver PW 6 and other circumstances. Abdus Sabur thus abetted in commission of crime. 

 54. Abdus Sabur, also, made himself liable to suffer conviction on the "last seen theory." Evidences had been highlighted from the mouth of PW 36 and PW 37, father and mother of Fatik, that Abdus Sabur and Fatik together came out from the house of PW 36 and by a baby-taxi proceeded towards Khulna and, thereafter, Fatik was untraceable. This incriminating circumstance unerringly points to the guilt of Abdus Sabur. 

 57. We now turn to examine the soundness of the contention advanced from side of Abdus Sabur in respect of discrepant statements of PW 36 and PW 37 on demand of Taka 5,00,000 or Taka 10,00,000 for the recovery of Fatik. Discrepancies which do not go to the root of the matter and shake the basic version of the witnesses cannot be annexed with undue importance, more so, when all probabilities factors echo in favour of version narrated by the witnesses. Again, human memory is admittedly very short and fleeting. Everything sinks into oblivion with passage of time. Every event as soon as it has happened soon starts fading in the memory. Contradictions and discrepancies are bound to creep in with the passage of time and, as such, much importance cannot be allowed to be attached to those unless those go to the root of the matter. Evidence of PW 36 and PW 37 in respect of telephone call of Abdus Sabur, telephonic conversation, arrival of Abdus Sabur in the house of PW 36 and discussion between Abdus Sabur and Fatik and their departure from the house and proceeding towards Khulna are consistent and not at all discrepant. Discrepancy in respect of demand of Taka 5,00,000 or Taka 10,00,000 is very much immaterial and that discrepancy could not and cannot destroy the prosecution version. The contention having been meritless stands rejected. 

 This takes us to the case of Ayub Munshi who stood convicted under section 201 of the Penal Code and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for seven years. True it is that he was in abscondence and tried in absentia but abscondence by itself does not necessarily lead to a conclusion of guilty mind. Even an innocent man may feel panicky and to evade arrest and trial he absconds when suspected of a grave crime like murder and disappearance of incriminating evidence. Abscondence can scarcely, be held as a determining link in completing the chain of evidence which must admit of no other reasonable hypothesis than that of guilt of the accused. 

 59. Like condemned prisoner Liaquat Lashkar and Jamai Farooq and convict-appellant Idris Jarnai there is nothing against convict Ayub Munshi except the evidence of approver PW 6 in connecting him in the crime. Prosecution signally failed to bring home charge against him and he can be, also, graced with a verdict of acquittal on finding him not guilty of charges mounted against him. 

 60. What sentence to be imposed upon condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder now demands consideration. True it is that Statute provides a discretion to Court in imposition of sentence for offence of murder and it is either death or imprisonment for life but that discretion is to be exercised in a manner and in consonance with concept of law so as to subserve ends of justice. In Halsbury's Laws of England it has been stated that exercise of discretion is a matter of prudence and not of law. In the case in hand evidence came forth that there had been a suspicion in mind of condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder that his wife Khodeja Begum had an illicit relationship with victim Fatik and this could have very well provoked him and that provocation might have reached to a boiling point resulting in the dastardly act. This can be characterised as a mitigating circumstance. Keeping in view this aspect of the matter, it could not be said that imposition of life imprisonment would not adequately meet the requirements of the case or that an imposition of extreme punishment i.e. gallows alone would do real and effective justice. Consequently, sentence of death may be directed to be modified into one of imprisonment for life.
